extracted.intended_audience: General literate readers of The Spectator (early 18th‑century English public)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles embedded in Spectator-style moral and literary essays on character, virtue, and the arts; aimed at producing or judging periodical moral discourse and related social commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: A very pleasant Fellow
rubrics_metrics.description: When pleasantness is accompanied by manly and virtuous sentiments it gives pleasing gratification; but when pleasantness stands alone and 'serves only to gild a Crowd of ill Qualities' the pleasant fellow is to be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warnings and examples: a pleasant fellow may 'turn your good Name to a Jest, make your Character contemptible, debauch your Wife or Daughter,' attend only to his own satisfactions, and purchase his pleasures at the expense of others; yet be socially welcomed. Distinguish pleasantness when paired with virtue versus pleasantness that masks vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pride and susceptibility to flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride is a universal passion that appears in many disguises and makes people vulnerable to flatterers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If pride is misapplied it 'lays us so open to Flatterers'; one who soothes our humour or temper gains 'an open Avenue to our Soul,' especially when the flatterer is our superior. Consider how vanity and the desire to be seen can be exploited; question whether pride does more harm than good and whether 'virtuous and laudable Pride' exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leader's genial familiarity — benefit and danger
rubrics_metrics.description: A sovereign's easy familiarity and delight in being seen can gratify the people's vanity and promote goodwill, but in the wrong hands can enable exploitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the example of King Charles II: his familiarity 'did him more Service with his loving Subjects than all his other Virtues' yet 'a Prince of this fortunate Disposition, who were inclined to make an ill Use of his Power, may have any thing of his People, be it never so much to their Prejudice.' Evaluate leaders' conviviality both for its social benefits and its susceptibility to misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate esteem by intrinsic (not apparent) value — Golden Scales vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not value things merely by their appearances; esteem and passions should be regulated according to real and intrinsic worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dream of the golden scales: weights (Honours, Vanity, Eternity, Time, Wealth, Poverty, Calamities/Blessings) reveal true comparative worth. Examples: a small 'Vanity' weight counterpoises large pomps; 'Eternity' outweighs Time, Prosperity, Affliction; an 'English Octavo' may be heavier than a 'French Folio' in real value. Practical rule: judge things by intrinsic merits, not surface glitter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunctions of qualities amplify value
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain qualities greatly increase each other's worth when combined (the whole can be far greater than the sum of parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed effects: 'natural Parts' weigh far more when combined with 'Learning'; 'Faith and Morality' reciprocally strengthen one another; similar pairings include 'Wit and Judgment, Philosophy and Religion, Justice and Humanity, Zeal and Charity, Depth of Sense and Perspicuity of Style.' When evaluating a person or work, account for synergistic enhancement from combined virtues or qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle condition / moderation best for gaining wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: The middle condition (neither extreme poverty nor extreme riches) is most advantageous for attaining wisdom and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poverty often focuses thought on supplying wants and can produce humility, patience, industry, temperance — but also envy, fraud, repining. Riches can produce humanity, good-nature, magnanimity — but also pride, luxury, and foolish elation. The practical ideal is moderation; biblical reference (Agur's prayer) counsels asking for neither poverty nor riches to avoid spiritual pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for strengthening and confirming faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and practices to secure a settled, durable faith in religion and conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptions include: when thoroughly convinced of a truth, do not continually call it into question; retain and, for the learned, memorize the strongest arguments that support belief (Latimer example, mathematician analogy); cultivate morality, since 'Faith and Morality naturally produce each other'; maintain habitual adoration (mental worship and outward forms) to produce experiential conviction; use frequent retirement and religious meditation to preserve impressions from the distractions of daily life (Aristotle and Psalm xix invoked).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for good dancing and dancers
rubrics_metrics.description: Dancing as an art should imitate nature, display beauty, and have motions appropriate to character; good dancing reflects understanding and can instill modesty and good breeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles: dancing's business is to display beauty — avoid distortions, mimicry, and contortions that raise aversion; motions should be 'proper to the Characters he represents' (example: Mr. Prince's character-based choreography that gives clowns clumsy graces); performers who wriggle, caper, or affect impertinent smiles are faulty. A good dancer must have 'a good Understanding'; dancing can be a mechanick method to implant good breeding, modesty, dignity, and virtues in young women (anecdote of a father's pride in his daughter's dancing).
